Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?
Introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next.
Read the paper
(opens in a new window)
00:00
Share
We’re introducing MedChemBench, a benchmark that evaluates AI models on reasoning tasks drawn from medicinal chemistry research. It tests whether models can connect a molecule’s structure with experimental evidence to explain results, compare compounds, and predict their properties. Building AI that can reliably support this work is one step towards helping scientists develop better medicines.
One of the hardest parts of this work is that improving one property of a molecule can make another worse. A compound might act strongly against a disease related protein but be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Medicinal chemists work through these tradeoffs by designing, making, and testing related compounds, then deciding what to try next. For AI to help, it needs to connect changes in molecular structure with experimental evidence and reason about what compounds are worth pursuing.
MedChemBench measures these abilities through 99 problems drawn from published research. At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT‑6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT‑6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. GPT‑6 Astra was strongest at reconstructing molecular structures and explaining experimental evidence. Selecting compounds and predicting their numerical properties proved harder for that model.
What MedChemBench grades
MedChemBench draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program: the biological target, the researchers’ goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings.
The benchmark evaluates four components:
Molecular structures.
Correct atom connections and specified stereochemistry in molecules assembled from the drawings and chemical groups provided.
Scientific reasoning.
Explanations supported by the supplied evidence, such as the reasons for choosing one compound over another.
Ranking and selection.
Compound rankings and choices that meet the stated requirements.
Property predictions.
Agreement with the numerical values and categories reported in the source material, including measured and calculated molecular properties.
Prediction across competing properties
One MedChemBench problem draws on research into inhibitors of PRMT5, a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and results from earlier experiments. It must predict how three related compounds will behave: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross a cell barrier, and how quickly liver enzymes break them down in a laboratory assay.
Later experiments, withheld from the model, showed a tradeoff. Compound 23 blocked PRMT5 in cells at a lower concentration, while compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay.
Predicting these properties together tests whether a model can connect molecular structures with several aspects of compound behavior. This reflects a central challenge in medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not necessarily come with better permeability or slower breakdown.
The benchmark checks whether the model reconstructs the molecular structures correctly and how closely its predictions match experimental measurements. Predictions receive partial credit based on their closeness to the measured values. Measurements already supplied in the prompt must also be reproduced correctly.
00:00
Small chemical changes can produce different property profiles. The task asks models to connect the structures with evidence about their behavior.
Testing spatial reasoning in medicinal chemistry
Before a model can reason about a compound’s properties, it needs to identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connections, ring structures, and stereochemistry.
MedChemBench tests whether models preserve this information when reconstructing molecules from the drawings and chemical groups provided.
One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the highest reasoning setting shared by all eleven models (xhigh), GPT‑6 Astra reconstructed this compound correctly in all ten responses. GPT‑5.6 Sol and GPT‑5.6 Luna failed across all ten responses.
In the illustrated answers, GPT‑5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, while GPT‑5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments.
These errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed. This example tests a foundation of medicinal chemistry reasoning: whether the model can accurately represent the compound before interpreting its behavior.
Figure 1. The same input, different molecules
These selected answers for compound 17 show a correct reconstruction, a smaller ring, and disconnected fragments.
While measuring the benchmark for structure components, Astra earned 95.4% of the available credit at xhigh. This result shows strong performance on reconstructing the molecular structures supplied in the tasks.
We evaluated eleven GPT models at different reasoning-effort settings. Across the full benchmark, Astra earned 83.3% of the available credit at the shared xhigh setting, compared with 82.0% for GPT‑6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT‑6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. At max effort, GPT‑6 Astra reached 83.8%. Higher reasoning settings improved scores, while large differences between models remained. The figure below plots performance against output tokens.
Figure 2. Performance versus token usage
Each point represents a model at one reasoning setting, showing 51 combinations across nine models from GPT‑5.6 onward. Scores are averaged across 99 problems; bars show 95% uncertainty intervals. Tokens include reasoning and the final answer.
The component results separate four abilities: reconstructing molecules, explaining findings, selecting compounds, and predicting measurements. This shows where models are strongest and where errors remain.
Figure 3. Component performance versus token usage
Component scores across reasoning settings. Token use is averaged over all 99 problems, as in Figure 2; bars show 95% uncertainty intervals.
Astra’s clearest strengths were in reconstructing molecular structures and explaining the scientific evidence. In selected reasoning examples from our preprint, Astra correctly identified structural changes and weighed their possible effects on protein binding, absorption, and metabolism.
Where selection and prediction remain difficult, Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh, but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. These categories use different tasks and scoring rules, but the results show substantial room to improve predictions and compound choices.
Where we go from here
These results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions. Prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out, and each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments. While the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery, its results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain. We believe MedChemBench will support continued progress and look forward to sharing updates as our models advance to serve the field.

Description
Palo Alto Networks is aware of the two Critical Severity vulnerabilities in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007.
CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free vulnerability in NGINX HTTP/2 proxy handling where active connections fail to clear their reusable state. When worker connection slots run low, NGINX can prematurely close and free memory for connections still actively proxying requests to upstream servers. This allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash worker processes or execute arbitrary code.
CVE-2026-123007 is an integer underflow vulnerability in NGINX HTTP/2 flow control where the flow-control window can exceed its allowed threshold. A remote unauthenticated attacker can send malicious HTTP/2 traffic to trigger a heap-based buffer overflow, crashing the worker process or executing arbitrary code.
Palo Alto Networks has completed its assessment and remediation for this NGINX vulnerability. Only on-premise products are called out below; any on-premise product not listed has been reviewed and determined to be unaffected. For cloud offerings, refer to the

items.title: 直播观察（三）：谁在直播间当榜一大哥，他们为什么掏钱？
items.content:
在前面的两篇文章中，我们主要介绍了
直播平台如何设计等级与盲盒等人工机制来诱导用户打钱
，以及
主播和榜一大哥如何围绕专属偏爱进行博弈
。但是这两篇主要是介绍平台规则和从业者的经验，这篇文章则会从真实的数据出发来看这些经验在现实中是否真的会成立。
动手收集数据之前，我们先翻了一遍公开的学术论文，发现已有的研究并不多。像 YouTube、Twitch 这样的欧美传统直播平台虽然有一些
追踪上百万小时虚拟主播的论文
，但它们和国内平台的玩法差异很大，主要靠付费高亮弹幕（俗称醒目留言）和频道会员赚钱，没有原生的抽盲盒和连麦比拼功能。而且欧美观众给主播的大额赞助大多走站外转账，公开网页上能抓到的站内记录相当有限。
如果直接把类似的结论套到国内，会产生很大的偏差。比如在我们采集的这批以中小体量为主的 B 站虚拟歌手与聊天直播间中，醒目留言仅占实付流水的 3.9%，超过 96% 的流水都是通过直刷礼物、房间包月会员（B 站叫舰长）和随机盲盒完成的。另一方面，国内确实也有
针对 270 万场 B 站直播的大规模打赏研究
，但它只抓了公屏上的文字弹幕和礼物账单，没有录制主播的声音做语音识别，也没法把主播说了什么和观众掏钱的过程对上号。
为了进一步弄清楚直播间里打赏的大哥到底是什么身份、又是因为什么原因掏钱，我们录制并转写了超过 1,200 小时的 B 站虚拟歌手与聊天直播音频。结合 74 万多条进房记录和 51.4 万元观众实付流水，我们用 AI 把谁在进房、在聊什么、什么情况下掏钱的全过程对上了号。结果还蛮出人意料的：从路人到大客户有没有一个销售漏斗、榜一大哥现实里究竟是什么身份、观众在什么情况下才愿意付钱，真实情况和我们的想象大不相同。
虚假的商业漏斗
作为一个互联网从业者，我看到直播间礼物结构时的第一反应是：这不是一个标准的转化漏斗吗？新观众先花 0.1 元点亮专属粉丝灯牌（后续继续送礼可升级），免费点 1 首歌；成为熟客之后，才舍得花 15 元抽心动盲盒去日常点歌。培养更多信任和依赖之后，有 138 到 198 元的包月舰长；到了两位主播连线比拼 5 分钟礼物积分的环节（打 PK），还会有几百上千元的重礼。
在现实中也确实看到很多新人主播每天都在求路人点亮一毛钱的灯牌。大家都相信只要把足够多的路人引进来，总有一些会变成舰长，变成榜一。但如果真的把 74 万多次进房记录和流水账单放在一起比对，会发现这个假设其实是错的。最明显的就是水面下庞大的沉默人群：接近 96% 的进房人次从头到尾一言不发，安静白嫖听完歌就走。而在掏过钱的 1 万多条观众记录里，按单个直播间里的消费角色拆开后，人数和流水呈现出明显的反差：

看表格的最后两行，73.2% 的流水是由单房累计消费满 500 元的核心大哥贡献的，这部分人占付费总人数的比例只有 1.3%；如果再加上只开通单月舰长的包月订户，这两类人加起来虽然人数只占 4.6%，却贡献了 85.9% 的流水。这提供了一种直接验证漏斗理论的方法：这批人数只占 4.6%、却撑住大局的舰长和大哥，是不是真的从最便宜的一毛钱过客一路升级上来的呢？
从上面这 1 万多条付费记录里剔除原本的老熟客，我们单独追踪了 3,600 多个以前没在房里升过灯牌等级、也没开过舰长的新付费观众，顺着时间看他们后来的消费情况，发现低价试水几乎不会往高价位转化，完全是一条听了就走的白嫖断头路。86.6% 的新客累计花费不到 5 元（绝大多数就是 0.1 元亮个灯牌换 1 首免费歌曲）就彻底停手了，加起来只占新客流水的 1.1%；另有 9.1% 的新客停在 5 至 99 元的点歌档。真正符合漏斗条件、从几毛几块钱起步，先抽点歌盲盒，最后一步步买到舰长或百元重礼的，只占新客的 0.4%。
换言之，超过 99% 的新客并没有走通这个漏斗。在这 3,600 多名新客里，前面这三档一共占了 96.1%，真正撑起新客大额流水的，是剩下的 3.9% 跳级玩家：他们一进门就绕开低价试水，直接买下舰长或百元重礼，一口气拿走了新客流水的 75.4%。在能看到全站荣耀等级的跳级新客里，超过八成的用户在进门前全站累计打赏就已经满 3,000 元（荣耀 25 级以上）。也就是说，他们只是今天刚逛到这个房间，这并不意味着他们是新手；在全站的其他直播间，他们早就完成了付费启蒙。中小直播间并不是从零孵化消费习惯的工厂，0.1 元买家的消费上限往往就是 0.1 元，大额流水靠的全是留住那些全站已经习惯掏钱的成熟玩家。
即使是小房间每天聊几百句话的活跃熟客，热闹的交流也不会顺着漏斗变成大额打赏。有个在欧洲律所上班的年轻法务，借着时差每晚下班后看国内凌晨的小直播间。他之前在另一位主播停播前冲动花过 1,000 多元，到了新房间却立下规矩，觉得欧元换人民币充值汇率太亏。跟播 11 场下来，他总共只花 27.6 元买小礼物捧场，光靠 400 多条聊异国日常、宽慰主播的弹幕，就混成了深夜场的熟脸。另一位凌晨看播的常客试抽过两发 15 元盲盒，结果只开出两个标价 9 元的小礼物，吐槽概率太黑后彻底戒掉盲盒。他平时送礼有近九成次数都只刷 0.1 元，只有在主播连续两天唱他点的免费歌，或者开玩笑吓到他后专门点名道歉时，才干脆掏钱买一张包月舰长。对这批清醒的常客来说，多发弹幕聊聊天就够换来陪伴感了，根本不会顺着盲盒和 PK 的漏斗往大户升级。
错位的榜一身份
既然直播间里的大钱几乎全是挂着高等级勋章的老熟客和跨房老手刷的，很多人自然而然会想，是不是天天泡在前排的这帮大哥，现实生活中全是一掷千金的富豪老板呢？毕竟在包月舰长不满 100 人的中小房间，超过 60% 的公屏弹幕都出自全站累计打赏满 8,300 元（荣耀 30 级以上）的大哥之口；对比之下，全站没花过钱的纯路人只发了大约 0.5% 的弹幕。但如果我们把所有有流水的直播场次按房间包月舰长人数分成三档，算一算当一晚榜一大哥到底要花多少钱，这层富豪滤镜就会碎掉一半。

把我们采集的这些虚拟歌房与聊天房合在一起看，拿下整晚榜一的花费中位数只要 249 元，而挤进当晚前三名的中位数只要 59 元。在大城市里，这两三百块钱连请同事吃顿像样的火锅都不够，回公司还得看主管脸色；但在几十人在线的中小直播间，这笔普通上班族咬咬牙就能掏出来的零花钱，足够包揽当晚过半流水，换来绚丽的进场横幅、满屋观众喊老板大气的捧场和主播几个小时围着你接话。
如果继续深扒这个看起来吓人的荣耀 30 级（全站累计消费 8,300 元），就会发现它也是时间叠加的结果。B 站官方规则是全站荣耀等级终身累加，只升不降。就算你连续 7 天没花钱导致勋章暂时变灰，只要在房间里随便刷个 0.1 元的小礼物就能重新点亮进场特效。普通工薪族每个月花 230 元左右，比如续一个连续包月舰长、顺手抽两三发盲盒，只要玩 3 年就能挂上荣耀 30 级的大佬头衔。翻看荣耀 30 到 39 级（累计打赏 8,300 元至 6.4 万元）熟客的 3,000 多场付费记录，高达 97.7% 的场次里他们整晚花费不超过 300 元，单场付费中位数只有 0.2 元。绝大多数晚上他们进房只花一两毛重新点亮进场特效、享受全屋欢迎，等到赶上连麦比拼或者聊到兴头上，才掏出一两百块钱点歌续舰。这完全是卡着月度零花钱过日子的花法，跟挥金如土毫不沾边。
顺着公屏上的日常闲聊往下看，这群人的真实身份就更清楚了。只发几句问候的过客看不出职业，但如果具体看累计花满 100 元、又在公屏聊满 300 条弹幕的真人熟客，荣耀 30 到 39 级的中腰部主力里有 82.8% 在闲聊中透露自己是普通上班族、倒班族或者在读学生，提到自己开公司或者有豪车别墅的是 0 人。即使看累计打赏 6.4 万到 33 万元的荣耀 40 到 49 级，也有一半以上（56.0%）是挤地铁、出差、算房租的白领和在校上课的大学生。真正时间和财务自由的富豪，主要集中在全站累计打赏满 33 万元（荣耀 50 级以上）的极少数塔尖玩家。有人刚坐十几个小时国际航班落地，还没倒时差就半夜钻进熟人直播间，卡着双倍积分连砸几笔 3,000 元大礼找乐子；也有 72 级的老牌玩家（全站累计消费满 570 万元）在半个月里给一个 60 多舰的腰部主播随手刷掉 2.4 万多元，一晚上抽盲盒亏几千元也毫不在乎，边玩手游边听歌互损，只求小房间里独一份的松弛感。
但这批塔尖玩家在我们采集的样本里一共只有 149 人，贡献约三成的总流水，剩下七成的真金白银全部来自累计消费 33 万元以下的观众。撑起这块基本盘的主力，正是普通工薪族、白领，以及住在大学宿舍里看直播怕吵醒室友的本科生和研究生。
而在这七成普通人中间，有一部分人非常精打细算，专挑小体量房间落脚，把在大房间不起眼的花费拆碎，换取最大的存在感。比如有位荣耀 37 级的上班族从不熬夜，坦言自己不是真大哥，常在清晨 6 点多进到只有十几个舰长的小直播间，抽几个小盲盒，让主播按顺序播他的私人怀旧歌单，自己一边听歌一边睡回笼觉，上午 11 点前下线忙工作。他 16 天里把 5,300 多元拆成 200 多笔小礼物，这笔钱在大房间连水花都看不见，但在这里却让他成了主播开连麦比拼前必须请示的头号靠山。
更让人唏嘘的是另一批打工人，他们把现实生活里的窘迫全投射到了直播间里。有个在外地大城市打拼的荣耀 46 级年轻上班族（全站累计消费满 18 万元），看到比自己大 1 岁的同事靠家里凑首付背上 20 年房贷买了房，觉得仅靠工资攒不下钱，于是对父母少报收入，自己当起月光族。哪怕第二天早上还要上班，他也在同一个 60 多舰的直播间里熬到凌晨 4 点，11 天砸下 5,400 多元，只为挤进房间榜单前排、换主播整晚接话的偏爱。还有一个 39 级的单休上班族租住在城郊，忍受着房东卡顿的无线网，所在的小公司资金吃紧，他入职 1 年没拿到年终奖，却在 40 来舰的歌房 14 天送出近 2,900 元参加午夜比赛。有一次刷完 50 多元礼物之后，只因主播漏叫专属亲昵小名，他就在公屏抱怨生分；在跟主播坦白当月没预算后还是停不下来连着刷，引得主播在麦克风里连声劝他注意控制。凌晨 3 点前，他自己也在公屏叹息说太容易上头。
最触目惊心的是一位荣耀 30 级的老面孔，在北方干倒班设备维护，早年跑过 81 天的日结零工，最近刚降薪到每天 210 元。父亲去医院做化疗那天，他送完身份证必须立刻返岗上班，怕请假休息影响挣钱。但在那个只有 12 个舰长的小直播间，他 16 天花掉超过 8 天的全额工资；哪怕充值触发微信支付的反诈风控限额，他也要 30 到 40 元一笔分批充进近 500 元，投进平台抽奖活动里（哪怕手气不好倒亏一百多元）博出一件 300 元的特效大礼攒在手里。等女主播正说着话，他抢在话音未落的瞬间把这份大礼甩在公屏上，就为换来一声措手不及的惊呼。
这种消费模式在传播学上有个专门的术语叫
补偿性消费
。在现实中，饭局上你穿什么衣服、开什么车、做什么职位，全都一眼能看出来；但一进直播间，弹幕面板把这一切都抹平了，观众只认你名字前的等级数字和当晚的礼物特效。那三成巨额流水确实有真的富豪在消费，但撑起大多数中腰部房间日常人气和包月流水的，往往是每天挤地铁、赶早班的普通上班族和学生。他们打赏未必是因为卡里多有钱，更多是因为直播间能让人尝到现实里很难体会到的身份反差：花两三百块零花钱，就能在下班后的两小时里暂时摘掉工牌，当一回全场捧着的贵客。
真实的掏钱瞬间
明白了台下大多数观众都有预算上限、会精打细算（即使是塔尖的真老板也不会无脑撒钱），就能理解为什么他们对每一百块钱都会斤斤计较，不会一进门就闷头刷礼。把超过 1,200 小时的主播语音转写和礼物账单对齐就会看到，观众从进门破冰、当晚掏钱到散场后愿不愿意回头复购，前后要经过三个环节：先要有话聊，再要遇上出手的理由，最后还要看当晚自己聊得尽不尽兴。
第一个环节是掏钱之前一定要先聊几句。很多人对直播间里神秘大哥的印象，是进场不说一句话、甩下几份大礼就潇洒走人。但在实测的 53 笔单次满 500 元的直刷重礼和醒目留言里，进房 1 分钟内直接砸钱的比例是 0%，超过九成在出手前都已经开口聊过天了。他们到底在聊什么呢？我们翻看掏钱前 3 分钟的观众弹幕，提前预告要送礼的不到 7%，将近九成都是在跟主播插科打诨、开玩笑。而观众本场还没花钱时，如果带着勋章进场弹出欢迎横幅，或者刚发出当天第一条弹幕，主播只要在 45 秒内叫出名字接上话茬，中低消费观众随后 5 分钟内掏钱的概率就会升到主播没接茬时的 3 倍左右。至于荣耀 40 级以上的大哥早就见惯了客套，打一句招呼不会让他们在 5 分钟内掏钱，得等后面的对局才会出手。
第二个环节是在聊热乎了之后，怎样给预算有限的观众递一个今晚非出手不可的理由。在包月舰长满 100 人的大直播间里，弹幕像瀑布一样滚屏，一般不打连麦比赛，主要靠舰长续费和醒目留言变现。而在包月舰长不满 100 人、平时打连麦 PK 的中小歌房里，主播卖力真唱、唱完道谢和曲间闲聊这三件事合起来占了全场 89% 的时长，但各自每小时平均流水却都只有 133 到 151 元；平时近九成时间的唱歌搭话，真正的作用是留住熟客在牌桌旁蓄水。一旦切到只占 11% 时长的连麦 PK 对战期，每小时流水立刻飙到 2,078 元，差不多是平时的 14 倍。
下面我们看看那 5 分钟的连麦到底是怎么催人掏钱的。平时主播在曲间随口劝大家点歌，随后 2 分钟平均只能收到大约 4 元；一旦进入 PK 喊话拉票，随后 2 分钟的平均进账立刻涨到 175 元（其中超过七成由荣耀 40 级以上的大户买单）。红蓝进度条、读秒加上双倍积分的划算感，让本来攥着两三百块钱犹豫不决的熟客一下子有了当全场救世主的心气。连麦冲分时，一旦有人刷出千元大礼触发全站顶部广播横幅（俗称飘屏），随后 3 分钟里确实会有大批看热闹的路人涌进直播间（平均每次多引来约 30 人次），但这批陌生访客平均每次飘屏加起来只掏 4.1 元。这也印证了之前
针对国内秀场直播的消费实验
：全站广播本来就不是帮主播拉新客的，它的真正用途是趁瞬间涌进来几十双围观的眼睛，替刚才掏出大钱的大哥当场兑现公开排面。
除了 PK 争面子以外，日常点歌还有另一个让人连续掏钱的开关，就是 15 元心动盲盒抽出来的不甘心。观众每花 15 元单抽一次，系统就会随机开出标价 2 元到 2,233 元不等的礼物送给主播。开出来的面值只要比 15 元贵就算赚了、有排面，不到 15 元就是账面亏了。我们统计了将近 1,000 次独立的单抽记录，发现开盒越惨观众越舍不得停手；就算只拿同一个人前后的抽奖记录对比，他在抽中最低一档标价 2 元的电影票后 1 分钟内咬牙补抽的比例，也比自己抽中保本或大奖时高出 23.4 个百分点。四档开盒结果对应的补抽比例如下：

大哥们找到了理由把钱花了出去，第三个环节就落在了散场之后。等观众真的把礼物刷出去之后，主播停下来长篇大论猛夸一两分钟，能换来下一次回头复购吗？答案是没用。单看本房老熟客，收到礼物后主播没专门点名寒暄，观众下次回访的比例是 75.5%；而主播停下来夸满 1 分钟以上，回访比例是 69.6%，并没有变高。
我们又看了 420 名在记录期内首场消费就满 15 元的观众，不管原本等级高低、当晚花了多少钱，主播收礼后猛夸一顿，都没办法让他们在后面的场次里更愿意回来掏钱。真正决定一个人下次还来不来花钱的，其实主要看他当晚自己在公屏发了多少条弹幕。马后炮式的客套留不住人，只有观众自己在房间里聊开心了，下次才会再进门。
翻完这批超过 1,200 小时的有声记录，直播间的玄学外衣也就褪干净了：这里没有把一毛钱的过客慢慢养成榜一大户的神奇漏斗，也没有遍地闭眼撒币的神秘首富；真正撑住整个生态的，是一群在全站跨房流动的老玩家，和下班后想花两三百块零花钱买两小时前排体验的普通人。他们进门先在插科打诨里确认屏幕对面是个聊得投机的活人，等气氛烘托到位，再顺着双倍积分读秒或者一张 2 元电影票的台阶把钱花出去。看清了观众兜里真实的预算，也看懂了他们掏钱出手的那一瞬间，直播间里那些眼花缭乱的勋章、盲盒和红蓝进度条，不过是顺着普通人的孤独与好胜心搭出来的精密机器。

items.title: Notes on Live Streaming (3): Who Are the Top Spenders, and Why Do They Pay?
items.content:
In the first two pieces of this series, we examined
how live-streaming platforms use artificial mechanisms like level badges and blind boxes to induce spending
, and
how streamers and big spenders negotiate over exclusive attention
. Those two articles leaned mostly on platform rules and industry insiders' experience. This piece turns to real data to see whether those rules of thumb actually hold up in practice.
Before collecting our own dataset, we reviewed the published academic literature and found surprisingly little to go on. Traditional Western platforms such as YouTube and Twitch do have
large-scale studies tracking over a million hours of VTuber streams
, but their monetization works very differently from Chinese platforms: revenue comes mainly from paid highlighted messages (Super Chats) and channel memberships, with no native blind-box gacha or split-screen PK battles. On top of that, large sponsorships for Western streamers often happen off-platform, leaving relatively little high-value data visible on public web pages.
Importing conclusions from those platforms straight into China produces huge distortion. Across the mostly small- and mid-sized Bilibili virtual singing and chat rooms we sampled, Super Chats accounted for just 3.9% of actual spending; more than 96% of revenue came from direct gifts, monthly room memberships (called
Captains
on Bilibili), and random blind boxes. On the domestic side, there is indeed
a massive study of 2.7 million Bilibili live streams
, but it scraped only public text chat and gift logs—without recording and transcribing what the streamer actually said into the microphone, there is no way to align spoken interactions with the exact moments viewers open their wallets.
To find out who the big spenders in these rooms really are and what actually makes them pay, we recorded and transcribed more than 1,200 hours of Bilibili virtual singing and chat audio. Combining that audio timeline with over 740,000 room-entry logs and ¥514,000 in actual viewer payments, we used AI to align who walked in, what they talked about, and what triggered each payment. The results were quite surprising: whether a sales funnel really turns casual passersby into big spenders, who the top-ranked patrons actually are in real life, and what moments make viewers spend all looked very different from what we expected.
The Myth of the Conversion Funnel
As someone who works in tech, my immediate reaction to a live room's gift menu was: isn't this a textbook conversion funnel? A newcomer pays ¥0.1 to light up a dedicated fan badge (which can later be leveled up with further gifts) and gets a free song request; once they become a regular, they spend ¥15 on a Heartbeat Blind Box to request songs; as trust and attachment build, they upgrade to a ¥138–¥198 monthly Captain subscription; and during 5-minute split-screen gift battles between two streamers (PK), they drop hundreds or thousands of yuan on heavy gifts.
In reality, plenty of new streamers do spend every session begging passersby to light up that ¥0.1 badge, convinced that if you pour enough newcomers into the top of the funnel, some will gradually climb all the way to Captain and #1 on the leaderboard. Put those 740,000+ room-entry logs next to the payment ledger, however, and that assumption falls apart. First comes the massive silent majority beneath the surface: nearly 96% of room entries never type a single word, listening quietly for free and leaving. And when we break down the 10,000+ viewer-room payment records by actual spending role inside a room, headcount and revenue diverge sharply:
Spending Role Inside the Room
Share of Paying Viewers
Share of Actual Revenue
Casual passersby spending under ¥15 (badges & small tokens)
86.5%
1.1%
Regular listeners spending ¥15–¥499 on blind-box requests (non-Captains)
8.9%
13.1%
Single-month Captain subscribers (under ¥500 total)
3.3%
12.7%
Core big spenders (¥500+ cumulative in the room)
1.3%
73.2%
Look at the bottom two rows: 73.2% of revenue comes from core big spenders who have spent at least ¥500 in the room, even though they make up just 1.3% of paying viewers. Add single-month Captain subscribers, and together those two groups represent only 4.6% of payers yet generate 85.9% of all cash. That gives us a clean way to test the funnel hypothesis: did this 4.6% of Captains and big spenders who carry the room really climb up step by step from the cheapest ¥0.1 passerby tier?
Filtering out existing room regulars from those 10,000+ payment records, we tracked over 3,600 newly paying viewers—people who had neither leveled up a fan badge nor held a Captain subscription in that room before—and followed their spending over time. Low-tier trials almost never convert upward; they are a dead end for free listeners. Fully 86.6% of newcomers stopped permanently under ¥5 (most paying just ¥0.1 for a badge and a free song), accounting for 1.1% of newcomer revenue; another 9.1% stopped in the ¥5–¥99 song-request tier. Viewers who actually matched the funnel—starting with pocket change, moving on to blind-box requests, and eventually upgrading to a Captain subscription or ¥100+ gifts—made up just 0.4% of newcomers.
In other words, more than 99% of newcomers never walk through the funnel. Together, those first three buckets account for 96.1% of the 3,600+ newcomers; the heavy spending among newcomers comes almost entirely from the remaining 3.9% who skip straight to the top—bypassing small trials on arrival to buy a Captain membership or ¥100+ gifts right away, and single-handedly taking 75.4% of all newcomer revenue. Among those jump-in newcomers whose site-wide Honor Level is visible, over 80% had already spent at least ¥3,000 across Bilibili (Honor Level 25+) before ever setting foot in the room. They may have wandered into this particular room today, but they are not beginners—they completed their spending onboarding long ago in other rooms across the platform. Small and mid-sized live rooms are not factories that incubate spending habits from scratch. A ¥0.1 buyer's ceiling is usually ¥0.1; big revenue comes from retaining mature spenders who are already in the habit of paying across the site.
Even active regulars who send hundreds of messages a night in small rooms do not naturally glide up a spending funnel. Take a young legal professional working at a law firm in Europe who uses the time-zone offset to unwind in late-night Chinese streams after work. After impulsively spending over ¥1,000 before a previous favorite streamer retired, he set a firm rule in his new room: converting euros into RMB to recharge was too bad a deal. Across 11 sessions, he spent just ¥27.6 in small tokens, yet became a core late-night regular on the strength of 400+ chat messages sharing stories from abroad and cheering the streamer up. Another late-night regular tried two ¥15 blind boxes, pulled two ¥9 consolation gifts, complained about the rigged feel, and swore off blind boxes for good. Nearly 90% of his gift clicks stayed at ¥0.1; he only bought a monthly Captain subscription when the streamer sang his free requests two days in a row, or apologized to him by name after teasing him too hard. For level-headed regulars like these, chatting actively already delivers all the companionship they want—they are never going to climb a blind-box and PK ladder into whales.
The Mismatched Identity of the #1 Patron
Since nearly all the big money in live rooms comes from regulars and cross-room veterans wearing high-level badges, it is natural to assume the people camping out at the top of the leaderboard are wealthy bosses throwing money around in real life. After all, in small and mid-sized rooms with fewer than 100 Captains, over 60% of public chat comes from users who have spent at least ¥8,300 site-wide (Honor Level 30+); by contrast, zero-spend passersby write only about 0.5% of chat. Yet the moment we bucket every revenue-generating session by room size and check what it actually costs to be #1 for an evening, half of that billionaire mystique shatters.

Median Session Revenue
Median #1 Patron Spend
Median Top-3 Threshold

Mid-sized rooms (30–99 Captains)
¥759

Large rooms (100+ Captains)

¥138
Across all the virtual singing and chat rooms we monitored, the median spend to take #1 for an entire evening was just ¥249 (~
\(35), and breaking into the top 3 took a median of ¥59 (~\)
8). In a major city, two or three hundred yuan barely covers a decent hotpot dinner with coworkers—and you still have to answer to your boss the next morning. Inside a small or mid-sized live room with a few dozen people online, however, that modest slice of a salaried worker's pocket money is enough to cover more than half the night's revenue, buying a flashy entry banner, a chorus of "generous boss!" in chat, and hours of the streamer riffing directly with you.
Dig into that intimidating-looking Honor Level 30 badge (¥8,300 cumulative spend across Bilibili), and it turns out to be mostly an artifact of time. Under Bilibili's official rules, site-wide Honor Level accumulates for life and never drops. Even if your badge grays out after 7 days without spending, tossing a single ¥0.1 gift lights all the entry effects right back up. An ordinary salaried worker spending roughly ¥230 a month—say, renewing an auto-pay Captain subscription and pulling a couple of blind boxes—will wear an Honor Level 30 badge after three years. Looking across more than 3,000 paid sessions by Honor Level 30–39 regulars (¥8,300 to ¥64,000 lifetime spend), in 97.7% of sessions they spent ¥300 or less for the entire night, with a median single-session spend of just ¥0.2. Most evenings they walk in, drop ten or twenty fen to light up their entry banner and enjoy the room's welcome, and only open their wallets for ¥100–¥200 when a PK battle breaks out or the vibe hits just right. That is strict monthly-allowance budgeting, nothing like throwing money around.
Follow the everyday chatter in public chat, and the real-life demographics come into even sharper focus. Casual visitors who only say hello reveal nothing about their jobs, so we focused on real regulars who had spent at least ¥100 and sent at least 300 chat messages. Among the Honor Level 30–39 backbone, 82.8% casually mentioned being ordinary office workers, shift technicians, or students—and exactly 0 mentioned owning a company, luxury cars, or villas. Even up in Honor Level 40–49 (¥64,000 to ¥330,000 lifetime spend), more than half (56.0%) were white-collar commuters worrying about subways, business trips, and rent, or college students attending classes. Genuinely wealthy players with both time and financial freedom are concentrated at the very tip of the pyramid—Honor Level 50+ (¥330,000+ lifetime spend). One had just stepped off a dozen-hour international flight and, still jet-lagged, hopped into a familiar room after midnight to drop multiple ¥3,000 gifts during double-points windows purely for fun. Another Level 72 veteran (¥5.7 million+ lifetime spend) casually dropped over ¥24,000 in two weeks on a 60-Captain mid-sized streamer, unfazed by losing thousands of yuan in blind boxes in a single night, playing mobile games while bantering with the streamer purely for the relaxed vibe of a small room.
Yet those apex players numbered just 149 people across our entire dataset, generating roughly 30% of total revenue. The remaining 70% of real cash came entirely from viewers below ¥330,000 lifetime spend—propped up primarily by ordinary salaried workers, white-collar employees, and undergraduates or grad students watching quietly in college dorms so they wouldn't wake their roommates.
Within that 70% majority, some are remarkably calculating, deliberately picking tiny rooms where modest budgets stretch into maximum presence. One Honor Level 37 office worker never stays up late and openly jokes that he isn't a real whale. He drops into a room with barely a dozen Captains around 6 a.m., pulls a few small blind boxes so the streamer plays his personal nostalgic playlist in order while he listens and naps, then logs off before 11 a.m. for work. Over 16 days he broke ¥5,300+ into more than 200 small gifts—an amount that wouldn't make a ripple in a large room, yet here made him the #1 backer the streamer checks with before starting a PK battle.
Far more sobering is another group of workers who project real-life squeeze straight into the live room. One young Honor Level 46 office worker living away from home in a major city (¥180,000+ lifetime spend) watched a coworker just a year older buy an apartment with family down-payment help and a 20-year mortgage. Convinced he could never save enough on salary alone, he underreported his income to his parents and lived paycheck to paycheck; even with work the next morning, he stayed up until 4 a.m. in a 60-Captain room and dropped ¥5,400+ in 11 days just to stay near the top of the room's leaderboard and hold the streamer's nightly attention. Another Level 39 worker with only one day off a week rented on the urban fringe with laggy landlord Wi-Fi at a cash-strapped small company that skipped his year-end bonus—yet spent nearly ¥2,900 over 14 days in a 40-Captain room on midnight PK battles. After sending ¥50+ once, he complained in chat that the streamer felt distant just for missing his personal nickname; even after admitting he was out of budget for the month, he couldn't stop sending gifts until the streamer pleaded into the mic for him to rein it in, and before 3 a.m. he sighed in chat that it was too easy to lose control.
The starkest case was an Honor Level 30 regular doing shift-based equipment maintenance in northern China, who once worked 81 days of day-labor gigs and had recently taken a pay cut down to ¥210 a day. On the day his father went to the hospital for chemotherapy, he dropped off his ID card and rushed straight back to his shift for fear of losing wages. Yet inside a tiny 12-Captain room, he spent more than 8 full days of wages over 16 days. Even when recharging triggered WeChat Pay's anti-fraud limit, he split payments into ¥30–¥40 chunks to push nearly ¥500 into a platform lottery event—absorbing over ¥100 in losses just to pull a ¥300 special-effect gift and hold it in reserve. Waiting until the streamer was mid-sentence, he fired it onto the screen just to hear her startled gasp.
Communication scholars have a name for this pattern:
compensatory consumption
. At an offline dinner table, your clothes, your car, and your job title are immediately visible. Inside a live room, the chat panel flattens all of that away—everyone sees only the badge number beside your name and the gift animation flashing across the screen. True whales do account for roughly 30% of the money, but the everyday traffic and monthly subscriptions keeping most small and mid-sized rooms alive come largely from ordinary commuters and students. They tip not because their bank accounts are overflowing, but because a live room sells a status inversion that real life rarely offers: for two or three hundred yuan of pocket money, you can take off your work badge for two hours after shift and be treated as the guest of honor.
The Actual Moment They Pay
Once you see that most viewers in the room have real budget ceilings and count every hundred yuan carefully (and even apex whales don't spend blindly), it makes sense why they don't walk in and start throwing money at the screen. Aligning 1,200+ hours of streamer transcripts with gift ledgers reveals three distinct stages from walking in, to paying that night, to deciding whether to come back: first there has to be a real conversation, then there has to be a reason to spend, and finally it comes down to whether the viewer genuinely enjoyed chatting that night.
The first link is that conversation almost always precedes payment. Outsiders often picture mysterious whales gliding into a room silently, dropping a pile of gifts, and vanishing. Yet across all 53 single-shot gifts and Super Chats of ¥500 or more in our dataset, exactly 0% were dropped within the first minute of entering, and over 90% of payers had already spoken in chat before opening their wallets. What are they talking about? Looking at chat messages in the 3 minutes before payment, fewer than 7% announce an upcoming gift; nearly 90% are casual banter and jokes with the streamer. When a viewer who hasn't paid yet enters with a lit badge banner or posts their first message of the day, if the streamer calls out their name and picks up the thread within 45 seconds, the odds of a low- or mid-tier viewer spending within the next 5 minutes jump to roughly 3x the rate when the streamer misses the cue. Honor Level 40+ veterans, by contrast, have heard every greeting in the book—a quick hello won't make them pay within 5 minutes; they wait for the right moment later in the session.
The second link, once the room is warmed up, is giving budget-conscious viewers a compelling reason to pull the trigger tonight. Large rooms with 100+ Captains have waterfall-speed chat, rarely run PK battles, and monetize mainly through Captain renewals and Super Chats. In small and mid-sized singing rooms (<100 Captains) that run PK battles, however, genuine singing, post-song thanks, and between-song banter together take up 89% of airtime—yet each averages just ¥133 to ¥151 per hour. Nearly nine-tenths of the broadcast is really about keeping regulars seated at the table. The instant the room switches into the 11% of airtime devoted to PK battles, hourly revenue spikes to ¥2,078—nearly 14 times the baseline.
Let's look closely at how those 5 minutes of PK actually move money. When a streamer casually asks for song requests between songs, the following 2 minutes bring in an average of roughly ¥4. Switch to rallying votes during a PK battle, and the following 2 minutes jump to an average of ¥175 (over 70% covered by Honor Level 40+ spenders). The red-and-blue progress bar, countdown timer, and 2x-score bargain logic suddenly make a regular who was hesitating over two or three hundred yuan feel like the hero saving the room. And when someone drops a ¥1,000+ gift during a PK push and triggers a site-wide broadcast banner, crowds of curious onlookers really do flood in over the next 3 minutes (averaging ~30 extra entries per banner)—yet those unfamiliar visitors spend a combined average of just ¥4.1 per banner. That echoes earlier
field experiments on Chinese showroom live streaming
: site-wide banners were never meant to acquire new paying fans for the streamer; their real job is to pull dozens of fresh pairs of eyes into the room right on cue to cash out public prestige for the patron who just paid.
Beyond PK rivalry, everyday song requests hide a second spending trigger: the sting of losing on a ¥15 Heartbeat Blind Box. Every ¥15 pull drops a random gift priced from ¥2 to ¥2,233 straight to the streamer—anything above ¥15 feels like a win with bragging rights, anything below feels like a loss. Across nearly 1,000 independent single pulls, the worse the unboxed item, the harder viewers found it to stop. Even comparing the exact same person against their own prior pulls, their rate of immediately pulling again within 1 minute after hitting the bottom-tier ¥2 Movie Ticket was 23.4 percentage points higher than after breaking even or winning big. Here is the 1-minute re-pull rate across all four outcome tiers:
Single ¥15 Blind-Box Outcome
Gift Sticker Value
Immediate Re-Pull Rate Within 1 Min
Jeweled Scepter & higher jackpots
¥40 to ¥2,233
12.5%
Heart Pillow (just broke even)
¥16
33.6%
Cotton Candy (¥6 loss)
¥9
42.3%
Movie Ticket (¥13 loss)
¥2
45.9%
Once viewers find their reason to pay, the third link happens after the stream wraps up. After a gift lands, does stopping the show to heap praise on the donor for a full minute or two make them more likely to return and spend again? The data says no. Looking strictly at existing room regulars, when a streamer didn't pause for an extended shout-out after a gift, 75.5% returned in a future session; when the streamer stopped to praise them for more than a full minute, the return rate was 69.6%—no lift whatsoever.
We also examined 420 viewers who spent at least ¥15 in their first recorded session: regardless of their Honor Level or how much they spent that night, lavish post-gift flattery failed to increase repeat spending in later sessions. What actually predicts whether someone comes back to spend again is how many chat messages they themselves sent that night. After-the-fact politeness doesn't keep people around; viewers come back only when they genuinely had fun talking in the room.
After combing through more than 1,200 hours of live audio, the mystique surrounding live-stream tipping dissolves. There is no magical funnel turning ten-cent passersby into whales, nor a roomful of effortless billionaires tossing money blindly. What actually holds the ecosystem together is a pool of seasoned spenders circulating across rooms, alongside ordinary people willing to spend two or three hundred yuan after work to buy two hours in the front row. They walk in, test through casual banter that there is a real human on the other side of the screen worth talking to, and when the atmosphere peaks, take the cue handed to them by a double-points countdown or a ¥2 Movie Ticket. Once you see the real budgets in viewers' pockets and the exact moments they decide to spend, all those dazzling badges, blind boxes, and red-and-blue progress bars turn out to be a precision machine built straight along the grain of ordinary human loneliness and competitiveness.

items.title: 黄仁勋辞职后的第一份财报：英伟达为何停发对华芯片，千亿担保又何时生效？
items.content:
2026 年 11 月 17 日美股盘后，也就是黄仁勋宣布辞职的第 5
天，英伟达发布了第三季度的财报。从业绩上看，这个算力的巨人仍在狂奔：单季营收
1158
亿美元
，同比增长一倍。同时，它还对下季度的营收进行了指引，目标是
1300 亿美元。
但在财报发布当天，接任临时 CEO 的首席财务官 Colette Kress
和董事会释放了两个新动作和一项关键披露：第一，美国政府还没吊销出口许可，英伟达就主动宣布停止向中国出口所有已获批的
Hopper
架构数据中心芯片，并在下季度官方指引里把对华数据中心计算收入清零。第二，面对近
20 万人联名要求迎回黄仁勋的请愿书和黄仁勋本人的复职表态，董事长 Harvey
Jones
在电话会开场就拒绝，并设立由前高盛副董事长挂帅的董事会国家安全常设委员会，收缴了公司合规团队的汇报线。第三，在提交给美国证交会的
CFO
评述附注
和电话会上，Kress 首次系统说明了 6680
亿美元承诺与担保中既有合同的生效边界，回应市场对英伟达替下游施工期兜底的担忧。同一份财报里，一边是管理层主动改了出货与治理决策，一边是投资者终于看清了千亿担保何时生效。华盛顿还没撤回许可证，新管理层为什么要自己关掉中国正门？而账面上不断膨胀的千亿担保，到底在什么条件下才会触发？
华盛顿还没吊销许可证，英伟达为什么要自己掐断单季
24 亿美元的中国正门？
上一个季度，英伟达获批对华销售的 Hopper 架构数据中心芯片（主要是
H200）为公司带来了
24
亿美元
的营收。在这次财报电话会上，Kress
直接宣布：「我们的指引里不再包含任何获批的 Hopper
数据中心产品，我们也不再向中国出货获批的 Hopper
数据中心产品。」公司没有披露停运的原因，也没有表态这个决定是否是永久的，但等待出口管制许可恢复已经不再属于英伟达的经营假设。
一家上市公司主动放弃仍在合规出货的渠道，首先是因为这其中的利润对如今的英伟达来说已经不重要了。这笔对华销售仅占英伟达上季度数据中心收入的
2.2%。而刚刚进入量产的新一代旗舰架构 Vera
Rubin，在投产的第一个季度就卖出了 200
亿美元，全球大型云厂商签下的不可撤销订单积压总额超过 2.5
万亿美元。台积电的晶圆和封装产能仍然紧缺，原来用来生产对华芯片的产能，转眼就能供给排队等货的欧美云巨头。砍掉中国正门不仅没有拉低业绩预期，Kress
反而将下一财年的营收增长指引上调至 75%。
更重要的是，这个看似不起眼的正门渠道，在交付和法律两个层面都成了定时炸弹。据路透社
11
月的报道
，由于国内进口审批配额和国产芯片配套要求，多达 60
万颗已获美国批准的 H200
芯片滞留在香港仓库。正规渠道受阻反而抬高了内地黑市价格，连早已在美国实体清单上的军工高校
西北工业大学
也通过境内中间商买到了这批
H200 芯片。
而在美国这边，这种发货机制的合法性也随着中期选举民主党夺回两院而受到审视。此前
H200
能获批对华出售，是因为黄仁勋和特朗普政府达成特殊安排：台湾造好的芯片要先运到美国做安全检查，再由美国政府按照《1962
年贸易扩展法》第 232 条征收 25%
关税，最后发许可证转口给中国客户。参议院财政委员会和众议院筹款委员会的民主党领袖近日
联名致函商务部长卢特尼克
，指认这种先绕道美国交关税再转口的机制属于违宪的出口税，并质疑为什么获批名单中有军方关联的空壳公司，以及这批许可证是否与英伟达向白宫宴会厅等项目的捐款
2600 万美元以上有关联。
就在英伟达公布财报的同一天，《华尔街日报》报道
美国证交会已经对其展开民事调查
，审查其对投资者的披露是否带有误导性。同一天，前中情局总监察长等
15
位国家安全专家也联名致信美国司法部长
，要求调查英伟达是否故意视而不见出口管制的违规行为。虽然很难用一个原因来解释所有监管动作和停运之间的因果关系，但对于
Kress
和独立董事而言，继续向香港仓库出货只会不断给证交会和司法部的调查案卷增加新证据。因此，不等政府撤证，自己先把对华正门关停，是新管理层成本最低的止损动作。
正门只有
24 亿美元，那新加坡子公司淡出的 1040 亿美元去了哪里？
如果跟中国相关的算力通道只有单季 24 亿美元的 H200
正门，华盛顿的监管风暴就不会演变成迫使创始人辞职的治理危机。真正让监管机构盯上英伟达信息披露的，是体量比正门大得多、长期挂在新加坡名下的离岸交易。
在财报发布的同一天，《金融时报》披露了英伟达新加坡子公司的
当地法定申报文件
。文件显示，在
2025 日历年里，经当地子公司入账的外部客户销售收入高达 1040
亿美元，约占当年英伟达全球账面收入的近一半。这里需要严格区分统计口径：新加坡近半的收入占比属于当地子公司的日历年账面口径，不可与上市公司财年的分部口径混用。而且新加坡子公司一年过手上千亿美元营收，留在当地的税前利润却只有
5300 万美元，实际运抵新加坡本土的芯片不到总量的
2%。新加坡扮演的是离岸签约与开票中枢：大批亚洲客户在新加坡签合同开发票，再把芯片运往马来西亚等周边国家的数据中心。
让美国证交会调查人员警觉的，是 2025
年夏季英伟达进行的一项会计口径变更。在原先按客户开票地统计的上市公司财报中，新加坡的收入占比一度上升到
22%。就在那个时期，美方查获了新加坡云厂商 Megaspeed
大量采购英伟达芯片再经由马来西亚机房转租给中国大模型的链条，美国商务部向英伟达发出质询并配合新加坡警方开展搜查。随后在
2025 年 7
月，英伟达把财报地区营收核算口径从客户开票地改为客户总部所在地，原本占总营收五分之一以上的新加坡随即从财报分部披露表中淡出。
英伟达对华算力正门停运与东南亚离岸侧门收紧机制
然而，这一修改并未阻止华盛顿对东南亚远程算力通道的封堵。最近，研究机构
Unemployment Labs 发布了一份开源模型权重的
底层硬件指纹取证报告
，发现
DeepSeek V4、月之暗面 Kimi K3 等前沿模型均在禁运的 Blackwell
芯片上训练过，而这些算力是通过租用东南亚的机房获得的。11 月 16
日，美国商务部发布了 117 页的
远程算力管制临时最终规则
。官方新闻稿罕见注明，这项规则由美国财政部与白宫国家安全委员会起草并指示发布，直接绕过了此前备受国会质疑的商务部长卢特尼克。新规要求向新加坡、马来西亚等
5 国出口先进 AI
芯片必须申请美国许可证，并给向中国企业出租大规模算力的海外机房下达了 90
天申请许可证的宽限期。至此，无论是 H200
的正门出口，还是通过新加坡开票、在东南亚出租算力的离岸侧门，都在这几天里同时走到了终点。
为什么
20 万人的请愿书和黄仁勋的复职表态，换来董事会一句无意迎回？
看懂了新加坡口径变更和东南亚侧门掀起的调查风暴，就能理解为什么英伟达董事会在这个时间点坚决拒绝黄仁勋回归。黄仁勋辞职后，外部请愿网站征集了近
20
万个签名
，其中包括超过 1
万名自称英伟达员工的联署，马斯克、比尔·阿克曼甚至特朗普本人都公开喊话挽留。黄仁勋本人在财报前夕也声明：如果董事会认为合适，他深感荣幸，并愿意配合独立调查。但董事长
Harvey Jones
在电话会开场就明确回绝，原话说：「英伟达董事会一致接受了他的辞职，无意恢复黄仁勋的首席执行官职务。」
董事会之所以把门关死，除了黄仁勋个人的下属丑闻与内控签字危机外，《金融时报》和路透社同日曝光的
家族介入
Megaspeed 内幕
，揭示了公司治理防线失守的程度。调查显示，黄仁勋的女儿
Madison Huang 本职是负责机器人业务的产品营销高级总监，却在 Megaspeed
触发美方调查后私下聘请危机公关公司（后转由英伟达公款买单），跨部门指挥公司为
Megaspeed
高调辩护，甚至把公司资深传讯高管踢出了包含总法律顾问在内的危机应对小组。与此同时，她的丈夫、前职业滑雪运动员
Nico Caprez 入职后在 4
个月内连升两级，出任负责亚洲国际云合作伙伴交易的总监及全球 AI
基础设施增长副总裁，多次飞往亚洲直接经手包含大客户 Megaspeed
在内的云交易。
创始人女儿与女婿在经手涉案客户的亚洲云业务的同时踢开传讯高管指挥对外辩护口径，这令上市公司的内控防线在证交会和司法部眼中形同虚设。如果董事会此时迎回黄仁勋，无异于向联邦调查人员承认公司放弃整改内控。因此在回绝黄仁勋的同一天，董事会正式设立了
国家安全与出口管制监督常设委员会
，请来前高盛副董事长
Suzanne Nora Johnson
出任主席，并规定公司内部的国家安全团队与全球贸易合规团队不再向业务高管汇报，改为直接向该委员会与临时
CEO Kress
汇报。唯有把合规汇报权收归董事会、把黄氏家族挡在决策圈外，董事会才能在联邦调查风暴前立起机构免责的防火墙。
承诺与担保总敞口膨胀到
6680 亿美元，英伟达的千亿担保到底何时生效？
在切割地缘政治合规与家族治理风险的同时，市场更关心财务官出身的 Kress
如何处理另一枚金融焦点：英伟达为其下游算力生态提供的数千亿美元承诺与担保。在
此前分析黄仁勋辞职的文章
里，我们曾预判这位在内部反对过千亿美元租约担保的老牌财务官接手后，大概率会收紧表外兜底与超长账期，不再拿现金流无底线补贴高杠杆客户。但这份三季报和电话会给出的实际答案略有不同：Kress
并没有撕毁或改写任何既有合同，而是把原本就写在协议里的生效前提摊到了台面上。在过去两年里，为了帮助新兴云厂商（例如
CoreWeave）和前沿模型实验室获得土地、电力和机房建设融资，英伟达签下了大规模的算力承诺与信用担保。
从三季报的现金流和承诺明细看，市场之所以追问这些条款，是因为数字膨胀得太快。尽管英伟达上季度盈利亮眼，自由现金流却只有
438
亿美元
，低于华尔街预期 130 多亿美元；应收账款单季升至 810
亿美元，平均回款周期拉长到 64
天，创下四年最慢纪录。与此同时，公司表内外的三类承诺与担保总额从上季度的
5305 亿美元升至 6680 亿美元：直接采购、租约与投资承诺 5180
亿美元，新兴云算力承诺 320 亿美元，以及 1180
亿美元的最高担保总敞口。
英伟达 6680
亿美元承诺与担保结构及既有生效条件分项说明
把
EX-99.2
财报附注拆开看，1180 亿美元担保敞口与 320
亿美元新兴云算力承诺各有独立的生效路径，不能混为一谈。1180
亿美元最高担保总敞口分为三项：给软银旗下 SB Energy 俄亥俄州 PORTS-Pike
园区（9 栋建筑、约 4.25 吉瓦电力，20 年租约专属部署英伟达算力给
OpenAI）提供的 1050 亿美元信用支持担保，95
亿美元电力与系统信用支持担保，以及 35
亿美元新兴云土地、电力和机房壳体担保。针对占大头的 PORTS-Pike
项目，附注明文写着担保按每栋建筑完工且可投入使用的进度分期生效（首栋预计在
2029 财年），敞口随建筑上线逐步累积，再在 20 年租期内随 OpenAI
支付租金逐步递减，目前尚未发生任何担保赔付。
另列的 320
亿美元新兴云算力承诺，才有融资、部署和验收的前置披露：合作方必须自行筹集资金采购设备，且相关算力完成部署、投入运行并通过英伟达验收后，承诺才正式生效；如果这些条件没能按期满足，承诺的金额与时间可能受影响，部分承诺可能缩减或取消。在
财报电话会实录第
12 页
，分析师追问这是新做法，还是原本就在做、现在才写清楚。Kress
明确否认改动条款，回答这既不是新条款，也没有修改任何内容（“Is it new?
No. Did we change anything? No.”）。她同时以 PORTS-Pike
为例解释，英伟达的多数担保都是在机房建成、准备投入使用时才开始生效，
她在电话会上说
：「如果这一切启动后，不幸出现延期或在建设中遇到困难，我们的担保就不再存在了。」她还重申，在扣除供应链和必要战略用途后，计划在
2028 财年末前用完剩余 2273 亿美元的股票回购授权。
算力基建最容易出问题的阶段，恰恰是拿地、拉电网、找银行借建筑贷款和盖机房的施工期。这份附注带来的新信息，并不在于新管理层临时改写了合同，而在于投资者第一次看清了既有契约的边界：施工期的融资与建造风险原本就留在合作方和放贷机构手里，英伟达并没有在机房完工前替下游无条件兜底。
把这一天的所有信号合在一起，英伟达权力交接后的轮廓就浮现出来了。黄仁勋时代的打法，习惯靠创始人亲自出面斡旋地缘管制、靠模糊的千亿生态叙事推高市场预期；而
Vera Rubin 首季 200 亿美元出货和 2.5
万亿美元的云积压订单证明，核心算力依然处于卖方市场，英伟达不需要冒合规风险也能卖光每一颗芯片。于是，同一份财报里呈现出两条清晰的变化：一边是高盛出身的委员会主席与财务官出身的临时掌门人主动止损，砍掉带有监管传染性的对华
Hopper
出货、把合规汇报线收归董事会；另一边是用更细的财报附注把千亿担保的既有边界讲透，打消市场对施工期兜底的疑虑。算力帝国的印钞机还在全速运转，只是那个靠创始人个人斡旋跨越政商红线的时代，已经在这份财报里转向机构化合规与更透明的风险边界。

items.title: 从内置收银台退回代填旧网页：OpenAI 为什么给 AI 办起了信用卡
items.content:
很多用户虽然经常使用 ChatGPT
来辅助购物决策，比如选品、比较参数，但在实际付款时仍然需要自己上网站输卡号，因为直接把真实的卡号给
AI 是非常不安全的行为。如果 AI
看错了买了别的东西，或者不小心泄露了卡号，就会造成经济损失。
2026 年 11 月 13 日，OpenAI
正式发布了
ChatGPT Wallet
，携手
Visa、Mastercard、美国运通和摩根大通，为刚刚推出的个人代理提供支付方案。一个多月前，OpenAI
在 ChatGPT
中推出了全天候个人云端代理，运行在一个独立的云端电脑和云端浏览器上，名为
dot
。
有了
ChatGPT 钱包
之后，你只需要在设置里绑定一次信用卡，就可以让
dot
在它的云端浏览器里，在商家网站上挑选商品、填写收货地址。在付款之前，
dot
会暂停并弹出一个窗口，提示你查看店名、商品、总价，并通过手机或电脑的面容识别或指纹进行确认。然后卡组织会在现场生成一个只适用于这一笔交易的替代卡号、安全码和有效期，也就是一次性代用卡号，交给
dot
填到商家网站的结账框里完成支付。
虽然看起来 OpenAI
终于支持了代理购物的付款环节，但其实它走的方向是完全相反的。以前 OpenAI
是想让用户在聊天框里完成购物和付款，现在则是由 AI
去真正的商家网站，在商家的结账页面上付款。回想 14
个月前那次把收银台搬到聊天框里的尝试碰壁后，这是 OpenAI
的退守。但在商家网站上付款，又带来了反欺诈风控、法律免责和店家封门这三道新门槛。
为什么不让用户直接在聊天框里付钱
每周 12 亿人用 ChatGPT，付费用户也近 1
亿。既然大家都在聊天框里问买什么好，最顺畅的设计难道不是在对话框里直接加个购买按钮吗？去年九月
OpenAI 确实这么干了。它联合 Stripe
推出对话框内置结账功能
Instant Checkout
，让用户不用离开聊天窗口就能直接点按钮付钱，OpenAI
则从每笔交易里向商家抽一笔佣金，当时还高调预告要接入超过 100 万家
Shopify 店铺。
然而这套内置收银台试了半年之后，今年三月就悄然关停，OpenAI
宣布将重心回归商品发现和比价。据 CNBC 报道，
根据调研公司
Forrester 的统计
，当初承诺的百万家 Shopify
商户，半年后真正上线的只有约 30
家。商家们算得明白：结账在聊天框里，商家只能在顾客付款后收到一张冷冰冰的订单，拿不到顾客逛店时的早期行为数据，也无法在结账前推荐顺手加购的商品。更致命的是转化率，沃尔玛实测发现，直接在
ChatGPT
聊天框里卖货的购买转化率，比把用户引回零售商自家网站结账低了三分之二。
不仅商家不配合，连消费者自己也没养成让 AI 代劳下单的习惯。今年秋季
Meta 的个人购物助手 Muse 登顶美国应用商店榜首，下载量破千万，但在
近期披露的三季度财报电话会上
，Uber
财务总监给出了一个让人冷静的数字：在全年最忙的万圣节那一周，全平台约 3.2
亿笔出行和外卖订单里，通过 AI 助手打车的总共只有 4 单，外卖也只有约 500
单。
其他生活平台也类似。DoorDash 每天约 300 万单配送中，来自第三方 AI
助手的订单总共只有几百单；Airbnb 和 Booking
的占比也微乎其微。原因并不复杂：在手机应用里自己叫车平均只要五十秒，复购常点的外卖只要一分半钟。人们愿意让
AI 帮忙搜资料、做对比，真到了掏钱那一秒，还是觉得自己点一下更省心。
不让商家改代码，代价转移到了哪里
既然商家不愿意改代码把收银台搬进聊天框，OpenAI
干脆把方向拧了过来。它的商业变现负责人
向
CNBC 证实
，
ChatGPT 钱包
在起步阶段对交易分文不取。在技术上，它不再要求商家接入新的收银接口，改成让
dot
拿着卡组织生成的一次性代用卡号，像真人一样去填商家网页上原本就有的信用卡表单。OpenAI
在同步发布的
《商户合作手册》支付指南
里直接写明：商家现有的结账页面开箱即用，不需要为这个钱包做任何专门的代码改造。
虽然商家不用再改结账页面的代码了，但只要付款请求一发出，就会立刻遭遇商家的反欺诈系统。一张卡组织刚签发的合规代用卡为什么会遭拒付？因为替你操作的
dot
并没有在你家里的手机上点按钮，而是在 OpenAI
机房的云端电脑上开着云端浏览器操作。在
Forter、Riskified、Sardine、Signifyd
等电商反欺诈系统看来，成千上万笔订单全都从同一批数据中心机房的网络地址冒出来，浏览器里又没有平时的历史记录，这和黑客用机房脚本批量盗刷信用卡的特征一模一样，风控系统天然就会把交易拦下来。
为了解决这个问题，OpenAI
在《商户合作手册》中明确指出，这种基于云端的浏览器有时会意外触发商家的反欺诈系统，导致付款失败。为此，OpenAI
提供了一套解决方案，让商家可以在 Cloudflare 等防火墙中识别 ChatGPT
官方浏览器的加密数字签名。此外，OpenAI
还在云端浏览器发送给商家的网络请求中添加了一个名为
Forwarded 请求头
的信息条，将背后真人的宽带网段、所在国家以及所在时区等信息传递给商家的反欺诈系统，以帮助其进行判断。同时，OpenAI
还与 Stripe、Adyen
等支付公司和四大反欺诈公司合作，修改了他们的识别规则。因此，尽管 OpenAI
声称商家前端零改造，实际上整个电商链条都需要在后台修改防火墙和反欺诈风控的放行逻辑。
内置收银台卡在商家不愿交出结账页，代用卡填表免去了代码改造却撞上机房风控拦截。
为什么每一笔都要你刷脸按手印
既然卡组织已经可以生成只能单次使用的一次性代用卡号，为什么 OpenAI
不让
dot
直接在后台购买东西，而要每次停下来要求面容或指纹确认一下呢？此外，在查阅
ChatGPT 钱包
的官方帮助文档
后可以发现，它的最初限制非常严格：只允许 200
美元包月的美国成年 Pro
用户使用；不允许绑定其他平台生成的虚拟卡作为资金卡，以防止虚拟卡套代用卡的追责断链；如果绑定摩根大通的卡，还要求必须是主卡持卡人而不能是副卡用户，绑卡时必须跳转回摩根大通的手机应用内完成生物识别审批。
把保护做这么厚，除了防黑客以外，更核心的原因藏在最新生效的
《ChatGPT
钱包服务条款》
里。如果 AI
在没有人类确认的情况下自己看错了尺码、买错了不能退的特价机票，这笔钱该谁赔？OpenAI
在条款里直接把话挑明：AI
系统可能会犯错，你在按下批准前必须仔细核对商家、商品和总价；一旦你点下批准，在法律上就等于你本人向商家发出了这笔订单指令。在随后的免责章节里，OpenAI
明确写明：商家才是唯一的法定销售方，OpenAI
不决定也不出资承担任何商家退款或信用卡拒付，并用全大写字母强调对钱包产生的任何购买、履约或争议不承担任何法律责任。
这种设计把责任划分得非常清晰。原来困扰整个行业的 AI
看走眼买错东西该谁负责的问题，通过付款前的刷脸就能解决。你按了指纹，在法律和银行系统里这笔交易就从
AI
的自动操作变成了持卡人亲手授权的消费。原有的信用卡积分、返现和买到次品时的拒付保障都还在，只是看走眼买错东西的风险也由按手印的你本人全盘接下。
真人刷脸在生成一次性代用卡号的同时，也将订单核对与售后争议责任留在了持卡人与商户之间。
商家要是连门都不让进怎么办
即使有了卡组织、风控公司和免责条款，另一个无法回避的对手是那些始终不希望
AI 代替人类顾客购物的商家。在
ChatGPT 钱包
出来之前，亚马逊就因为 AI
不看网页广告、不点击购买推荐而封锁了外部的购物助手。到了
ChatGPT 钱包
发布的两天前，商家们进一步升级了防御措施。11
月 11 日，
美国联合航空发布公告
，更新了网站的法律条款，全面禁止未经授权的任何第三方
AI 代理查票、订票或值机。美联航的条款几乎是对 OpenAI
的精准封杀：它规定只要使用了自动代理，不论是否有真人监督、即使每一笔交易都有真人批准，也一律视为违约。甚至加入了一个不放弃权利的条款，声明即便美联航的技术未能拦截，已经收取用户付款并发行了机票，也保留事后作废机票并追索的权利。
碰上不肯开门的商家，OpenAI
的官方文档其实暗藏了两条路：一条是面向商家的《商户合作手册》，它规规矩矩劝商家认领刚上线的
ChatGPT
商家主页、上传商品目录、在防火墙里放行云端浏览器；另一条是面向消费者的
dot
入门帮助文档
，它悄悄指出一条后门，如果某个网站封锁了云端浏览器，你可以开启桌面客户端的本地电脑权限，让
dot
借用你电脑上的本地浏览器去访问。前门讲合规合作，后门教借壳绕行，这恰恰说明单靠发一张合规的代用卡，还不足以让强势商家主动把门推开。
有趣的是，就在
ChatGPT 钱包
发布的那一天，Brave
浏览器宣布它的搜索接口支持一个新的功能，可以让 AI
代理在没有注册账号的情况下调用搜索，每次调用时直接在网络请求中附带 0.005
美元的链上稳定币。一手交钱，一手拿结果。这其实就是现在流行的
x402
协议
。但 Brave
的开源网关说明中也提到，它不得不移除了自动补全和拼写检查这两个接口，因为这两个接口的单次查询价格低于链上结算的手续费。
同一天的两场发布，把 AI
花钱的边界划得一清二楚：机器在后台向机器买半美分的数据，走的是免开户、不可逆的微支付；而机器替人去买几百块的机票和球鞋，容不下买错单的损失，只能退回传统卡组织网络，靠人类每笔刷脸按手印来锚定责任。OpenAI
折腾了 14
个月，终于用一次性代用卡号解决了怎么安全地把卡递给收银台；但只要商家还在担心失去流量入口、人类还得自己为订单核对兜底，离你彻底甩手让
AI 去网购的日子就还早得很。

items.title: nginx2root: RCE in nginx
items.content:
nginx2root is Xint’s name for five nginx vulnerabilities and a separate Linux kernel flaw. Each nginx vulnerability can lead to code execution as the nginx worker, under a specific configuration.
CVE-
2026-123007
affects unpatched nginx builds with HTTP/2 enabled and has been in nginx since 2015. Xint chained it with the kernel flaw to get root on the host, including from inside a Docker container where SCTP was reachable. Fixes shipped on 18 November 2026 in nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7.
Who is affected
Each nginx vulnerability is a separate attack path. The table lists the first affected upstream release, from F5’s advisories. Fixed releases are 1.30.7 on stable and 1.31.9 on mainline; distribution backports may also contain the fixes.
CVE
Affected configuration
First affected
CVE-
2026-123007
HTTP/2 enabled
1.9.5
CVE-
2026-123633
HTTP/2 proxied to a backend, worker low on
worker_connections
1.19.7
CVE-
2026-121810
HTTP/3 (Xint’s path: requests forwarded to a backend)
1.25.0
CVE-
2026-123634
Variable server name in
proxy_pass
, plus an SSI or
mirror
subrequest resolving it
0.6.18
CVE-
2026-113425
Mail proxy (Xint’s path:
proxy
on
and
auth_http
)
0.5.33
In Xint’s demonstrated chain, the kernel flaw is exploited after the attacker gains code execution as an nginx worker. It is a use-after-free in SCTP, present since Linux 4.15, with no CVE or kernel patch as of Xint’s disclosure. Whether it is reachable depends on the kernel, its modules and any container restrictions, and many distributions load the SCTP module the first time a program opens an SCTP socket.
How to check
These checks cover
CVE-
2026-123007
. For the other four, compare your configuration with the table above. Run each command against the binary and configuration the service actually uses: containers, appliances and custom builds may have their own.
Check the version with
nginx
-v
. Versions 1.9.5–1.30.6 and 1.31.0–1.31.8 are vulnerable, but distributions often backport fixes without changing this version, so compare the full package version with your distribution’s advisory.
Check whether the binary includes HTTP/2:
Terminal window
nginx
-V
2>&1
|
grep
-q
--
'--with-http_v2_module'
&&
echo
present
||
echo
absent
Check whether the configuration enables HTTP/2. The command joins each directive onto one line first, since a directive can span several lines.
nginx
-T
reads the configuration on disk, so it doesn’t prove the running workers have loaded it:
Terminal window
sudo
nginx
-T
2>&1
|
sed
's/#.*//'
|
tr
'\n'
' '
|
tr
';'
'\n'
|
grep
-E
'(^|[[:space:]{])listen[[:space:]][^;]*[[:space:]]http2([[:space:]]|$)|(^|[[:space:]{])http2[[:space:]]+on[[:space:]]*$'
From outside your network, check whether HTTP/2 is negotiated:
Terminal window
openssl
s_client
-connect
HOST:443
-servername
HOST
-alpn
h2
</dev/null
2>
&
1
|
grep
-E
'ALPN protocol:|No ALPN negotiated'
ALPN protocol: h2
confirms HTTP/2 at the endpoint you reached. If a CDN or proxy sits in front, test the nginx server directly too. No output or a failed handshake is inconclusive. This check also doesn’t cover HTTP/2 over cleartext.
What to do
The demonstrated chain has two stages. Patch nginx to block initial access, and mitigate exposure to the kernel flaw:
Update nginx
Update to nginx 1.31.9 (mainline) or 1.30.7 (stable), or a distribution package that lists these CVEs as fixed. For F5 products, use the fixed versions below.
Restart nginx or do a live binary upgrade. A configuration reload does not replace the running binary.
If you can’t update yet
These are Xint’s mitigations. They block the known attack paths but don’t fix the bugs.
For
CVE-
2026-123007
and
CVE-
2026-123633
, disable HTTP/2 on affected ports:
On 1.25.1 and later, set
http2
off
;
and remove any
http2
parameter from
listen
directives.
On older versions, remove
http2
from
listen
.
Check every server block that shares the same address and port.
Then run
nginx
-t
, reload, repeat the ALPN check above and confirm the site still loads over HTTPS.
Services that need HTTP/2, such as gRPC, will break.
For
CVE-
2026-121810
, remove the
listen
directives that contain
quic
, set
http3
off
;
and replace any header advertising HTTP/3 with
Alt-Svc: clear
(
add_header
Alt-Svc
'clear'
always;
). Then check that nginx no longer listens on UDP on each port your QUIC listeners used, for example with
sudo
ss
-lunp
'sport = :443'
. If the output still shows nginx, a QUIC listener is active.
For
CVE-
2026-123634
, point
proxy_pass
at a fixed
upstream
group instead of a variable. Setting
mirror_request_body
on
;
stopped Xint’s exploit, but doesn’t fix the bug.
For
CVE-
2026-113425
, keep untrusted clients away from the mail proxy by binding it to loopback or restricting it with a firewall.
A reload only applies a change to new connections. If workers still show
worker process is shutting down
, restart nginx.
Mitigate the kernel flaw
On hosts that don’t use SCTP, stop the module loading until a kernel fix ships: add
install sctp /bin/false
to a
.conf
file in
/etc/modprobe.d/
. This stops modprobe from loading the module. It doesn’t unload a module that is already loaded, and doesn’t disable SCTP built into the kernel.
Fixed versions
These are from F5’s five advisories, linked under References. NGINX Plus fixes vary slightly by CVE, and 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 cover all five. BIG-IP, BIG-IQ and F5OS are not affected.
Product
Fixed in
Not fixed
nginx Open Source

We checked the Linux distributions’ trackers for
CVE-
2026-123007
on 20 November 2026 at 14:00 UTC:
Ubuntu has fixed nginx on 16.04 to 26.10, through Ubuntu Pro on 16.04, 18.04 and 20.04. See
Ubuntu’s
CVE-
2026-123007
page
.
Red Hat has fixed nginx on RHEL 10 (RHSA-2026:100744), and still marks RHEL 8 and 9 “Affected”. See
Red Hat’s
CVE-
2026-123007
page
.
These statuses change quickly. Check each tracker directly before acting.
What to monitor
Look for commands started by the nginx worker, the strongest sign of a successful attack. Xint gives an
auditd
rule for
execve
()
by the worker’s user; other processes run as that user too, so check each event’s parent process.
Weaker signs, each with normal causes, are long-lived connections where inbound bytes keep climbing while nginx sends little back, many short TLS connections from one IP and worker crashes (
signal 11
in
error.log
). Investigate when several appear together.
Access logs don’t record the HTTP/2 frames this attack uses, and patching doesn’t tell you whether a system was compromised before the update.
Timeline
16 October 2026
Xint reports the vulnerabilities to F5 through HackerOne
10 November 2026
Xint validates the nginx team's patches
18 November 2026
nginx releases 1.31.9 and 1.30.7; F5, Xint and Rapid7 publish, with Rapid7's proof of concept
watchTowr reported no exploitation in the wild in its FAQ, last updated 18 November. As of 20 November, none of the CVEs is in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
Rapid7’s public proof of concept gets code execution on a fresh nginx 1.31.8 container by sending about 128 GB of HTTP/2 data, which takes 2 minutes on a 10 Gbit/s link. Rapid7 expects that approach to fail below about 300 Mbit/s, since nginx closes connections after an hour, and against a busy server or through a proxy. Those are limits of its exploit, not of the bug. Xint has withheld its own exploits.
Technical summary
CVE-
2026-123007
is an integer underflow (CWE-191) in HTTP/2 flow control. When streams with queued data close, nginx refunds their reserved send-window credit without rechecking the limit, so an attacker who has already raised the window can push it past its maximum. A later bounds check then underflows, letting the window grow to almost any 64-bit value, which nginx turns into a huge length for a memory copy. The result is a heap read and write that can leak addresses and overwrite a function pointer. F5 says code execution needs ASLR disabled or bypassed.
The other four are use-after-free bugs, in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connection handling under connection pressure, DNS resolution during subrequests and the mail proxy’s authentication.
In the kernel flaw, an SCTP association can be moved to another socket while a send is waiting, then freed, which Xint used to leak kernel addresses and call a kernel function of its choice.

nginx security advisories
F5:
K000163926 (
CVE-
2026-123007
)
,
K000163928 (
CVE-
2026-123633
)
,
K000163925 (
CVE-
2026-123634
)
,
K000163927 (
CVE-
2026-121810
)
,
K000163931 (
CVE-
2026-113425
)
Xint: nginx2root
Rapid7:
CVE-
2026-123007
analysis
watchTowr: nginx2root FAQ
F5 credits Xint for all five nginx vulnerabilities. It also credits Rapid7’s Stephen Fewer, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for
CVE-
2026-123007
, and Metnir, Wiz Research and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for
CVE-
2026-123633
. Xint’s researchers @imssm99, @cdor1, @tjbecker and @yves found the kernel flaw.

items.content:
A little over half a year ago, I wrote an essay reflecting on this topic: "
The Efficiency Paradox of the AI Era: When Greater Productivity Only Leaves Us Exhausted
." Back then, I asked: in the age of AI, when productivity was supposed to be liberated, why is everyone feeling more exhausted than ever?
Over the past half-year, this trend has become increasingly obvious.
Deep, focused mental work has increasingly fractured into constant context switching across multiple projects.
It feels like we have all developed ADHD in this era, struggling to stay focused on any single thing for long.
And the more capable models become, the worse it gets: we rarely work on just one thing anymore; instead, we juggle several concurrently.
Most people are the same way, running multiple side projects at once. Building things has become almost trivial—you can easily crank out several in a single day.
On top of that, the breakneck pace of AI has made us deeply dependent on it. Now, even just kicking off a new project requires an assist from AI.
"Building It" Doesn't Mean Skill
Model progress over the past half-year has been blistering—GPT 5.4 is already an eight-month-old model.
Meanwhile, Chinese models have been playing catch-up, and by now they are at least on par with GPT 5.4. Just a few months ago, people were still debating whether hitting 5.4 would be enough to be satisfied.
With models as capable as they are now, technical barriers have largely vanished, and what people jokingly call "wishful programming"—prompting an app into existence—has become all the rage. Even a complete novice can build an app that basically meets requirements, though it might not be very good to use.
To be fair, the rapid rise of AI has let more people experience the joy of building software and create tools that help their daily lives or work—and that is genuinely meaningful.
But churning out endless garbage apps purely for hype, trend-chasing, and plagiarism is both shameful and sad.
"Building It Well" Doesn't Mean It's Valuable
In this environment, design and usability still matter immensely to me. An outsider might not grasp design philosophy or have much aesthetic sense. And among the flood of AI-generated apps everywhere, the vast majority are simply garbage.
This breakneck pace of iteration completely bypasses traditional development workflows. Design is no longer an upfront requirement in an AI workflow; it might even be outsourced entirely to whatever taste the model has. Does that mean design no longer matters?
Even apps from top-tier Chinese tech giants can leave you deeply skeptical of their aesthetics once you try them. Take Tencent's Work Buddy: daily active users have already topped 10 million, yet when I opened it with a sense of reverence, taking in its UI, visual texture, and usability, all I could call it was garbage.
Granted, perhaps that is because I consider myself a design engineer and have a heightened sensitivity to UI details.
In a climate like this, have people simply stopped caring about whether software is intuitive and beautiful?
Most users do not care about this at all. Even if the UI is hideous, the UX is clumsy, and performance is completely ignored—so long as it barely works, many users have begun to compromise, or just stopped caring altogether in this AI wave. As long as it gets their work done and delivers what they want, that is all that matters.
Examples like this are everywhere. With so many apps, you have no idea why the interface is so ugly or what the software is even supposed to help you do, yet it still manages to blow up with insane hype in this climate.
When total novices who know nothing about software engineering, architecture, or design can use marketing tactics to churn out a completely pointless piece of garbage, I find that a tragedy of our era.
Meanwhile, craftsmen who tirelessly polish a product, pouring in genuine ideas, design sensibility, and intuitive usability, get neither the recognition nor the respect they deserve—buried and forgotten simply because their growth tactics fell short. That, too, is a tragedy.
In an era like this, does it even make sense to build a product with care anymore?
The other end takes the exact same shape: in products, aesthetics are pushed behind whether something can be built at all; in models, the top-tier capabilities are consolidating into just a few companies. You have more and more to choose from, but fewer and fewer things that are actually good.
"The Best" Doesn't Mean It's Yours
Once you have used frontier models, though, your appetite is endless. Looking back, even 5.4, as the cutting-edge model of its time, was more than capable of handling most of our daily work—and today, domestic Chinese models have long surpassed that benchmark.
Constrained by compute and tightening US export controls, domestic models still face an uphill battle against America's frontier. The window to catch up is shrinking, and the frontier is moving at breakneck speed—releasing a new generation every month is considered slow, and competing labs sometimes drop two in a single month. Naturally, everyone still wants to use the most advanced models, but here in China, actually using them is only getting harder.
Among frontier model labs, OpenAI has been relatively consumer-friendly and less restrictive with regional geoblocking, but its flagship models are noticeably falling behind Anthropic's. That strikes me as a sad state of affairs. In the closed-source space, Anthropic essentially stands alone at the top right now; while Gemini and OpenAI keep trying to close the distance, the gap still feels immense.
And Anthropic happens to be a deeply anti-human organization. It feels like they just want to play dictator in the AI era, wishing nobody else would make models unless it fits the utopian society they want to construct—which is why they don't want open-weight models to evolve.

items.title: 让 Agent 先问清楚、画出来、再证明：我的 Ryugi 工作流
items.content:
Ryugi (流儀)
—Ryugi is a set of interactive artifacts I built for coding agents. Whenever the agent needs to ask me questions or have me pick an approach, it puts them on interactive pages where I can answer directly: design decisions are written up as a document where I choose options item by item and leave sentence-level comments; UI proposals are laid out on a canvas for me to click and choose; and when the work is done, an acceptance page places approved designs side by side with live screenshots so I can approve or reject them group by group. Every choice I make on these pages feeds right back into the agent session that started it.
Repository
· Innei
569
ryugi
Ryugi (ryoo-ghee) — artifacts for coding agents: artboards of mockups, design docs, whiteboards, HTML benches and verify reports you comment on, with every comment sent back to the agent. Install artifacts only, or the full brainstorm → spec → TDD workflow. Claude Code, Codex and more.
JavaScript
The project here was the whiteboard inside my blog editor, haklex. Its editing features had always leaned on Excalidraw, which pulled in a heavy bundle and clashed with the rest of the editor's visual style. I wanted to drop the dependency and roll our own whiteboard around Excalidraw's data format, without touching a single field in existing articles.
From my opening sentence to `git push` took about half a day: two rounds of development, one release, and three downstream projects updated. I typed fewer than 20 messages in chat; wherever I had to make a call, it was turned into questions in a doc or mockups on a canvas. Here is how it went, step by step.
After one prompt: a doc that asks questions
My opening prompt was just one sentence: "Drop the excalidraw dependency and roll our own whiteboard based on its data structures."
The agent first inspected the code to confirm the scope of changes, then opened a design doc and put its questions directly into it, without following up in the chat box.
The questions were embedded right inside the document, each with a recommended option and the reasoning behind it; all I had to do was click my choice on the page. The first question was a fork in the road that determined how big v1 should be—everything that followed depended on it. For two of the questions I skipped the recommendation, and the next round simply picked up from what I chose.
After each round, the conclusions were merged into a "Decided" section, noting whether I made the decision or the agent made it for me. I could tell at a glance which items needed another look.
Section 4 of the design doc, "Decided": each conclusion is tagged with who decided it
After two rounds, the document was fleshed out into a full design spec. Before handing it back to me, the agent had an uninvolved reviewer agent do a cold read; it resolved most of the feedback on its own, leaving just two questions for me to settle.
自研白板编辑器：替换 @excalidraw/excalidraw · Ryugi
View “自研白板编辑器：替换 @excalidraw/excalidraw” on Ryugi Cloud, a document artifact.
Ryugi
"Should we discuss the UI?"
Once the document Q&A was done, I asked: "Should we discuss the UI?" The agent said yes—the design spec had marked the UI as "left to the implementer," but these are things you see every time you open the editor.
Text doesn't do UI justice, so it switched to a visual canvas: each group presented several options side by side, the recommended one highlighted with a red border, and sticky notes explaining the reasoning right beside them.
Round 1 decision fork on the UI canvas: three layout options side by side, with the recommended one outlined in red
Across two rounds and five groups, I went with the recommendations every time. With the options drawn out side by side, it was immediately clear which were good and which were bad. The selected mockups were linked into the design spec to guide both implementation and acceptance. Then I replied with "approve."
白板编辑器界面 · Ryugi
View “白板编辑器界面” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Once approved, I didn't look at code again
Once approved, the agent broke the design spec into 19 small tasks and tackled them one by one on a separate branch.
Each task followed the same rhythm: write a failing test, watch it fail, write the implementation to make it pass, and commit. Whenever the agent made a call on its own—like minor details that diverged slightly from the spec—it logged it in a ledger. When the chat grew too long and was summarized, it kept working right from that ledger.
For over an hour, I didn't type a single word.
Review, then the acceptance page
Once all 19 tasks were finished, the agent handed the branch over to an independent reviewer agent that had played no part in development. For every issue flagged, it reproduced it with a failing test before writing the fix.
Then it spun up the editor in a real browser, took screenshots and screen recordings, and put together an acceptance page: my approved canvas designs on the left, and how it actually looked running on the right.
Acceptance page: approved design, live screenshot, and screen recording side by side
All I had to do was review each group and approve or reject it. I left a comment on one mockup; it made the fix, took a new screenshot, and placed it right back in the same spot for me to review. Anything it couldn't verify was listed separately on the page, instead of being mixed in with "Completed."
白板编辑器界面 · Ryugi
View “白板编辑器界面” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Round two: starting from a reference image
Next, I wanted the whiteboard to look sharper. I pasted a reference image featuring clean headings, drop-shadowed sticky notes, and illustrative stickers, and asked whether stock Excalidraw could pull off that aesthetic.
It broke down the elements in the image one by one—what we could already draw, what capabilities were missing—and even guessed I might want an AI to do the drawing. I replied with one sentence: only build general-purpose drawing capabilities.
Next was the same process: open a new design doc, then three rounds of Q&A. In round three, putting rich-text cards on the whiteboard was my own idea. After a cold read, the reviewer agent flagged two questions that needed my call; the agent added its recommendations, I replied with two numbers, approved, and let it implement and review.
The acceptance page for this round measured directly against my reference image: the reference on the left, the recreation inside our editor on the right.
Round 2 acceptance: reference image side by side with the in-editor recreation
白板绘制能力扩展：阴影、SVG 元素、富文本卡片 · Ryugi
View “白板绘制能力扩展：阴影、SVG 元素、富文本卡片” on Ryugi Cloud, a document artifact.
Ryugi
Verify · 白板绘制能力扩展 · Ryugi
View “Verify · 白板绘制能力扩展” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Release, then downstream projects
With both rounds approved, I asked: "Can we release now, and then adapt the downstream projects?" It cut a new release, then went through three projects using the editor one by one—bumping the dependency, running tests, and verifying in a browser that the whiteboard rendered properly.
Downstream results were posted right on the acceptance page as well, with one screenshot for light mode and one for dark.
The same whiteboard in downstream projects: light and dark mode
Throughout the entire process, logging in to authenticate the npm release was the only thing that needed my manual login—that was the one step the agent couldn't do for me.
What I actually said in the chat
Looking back, nearly everything I typed in chat over that half-day is captured right here:
Time
What I said
What happened next
12:26
Drop the excalidraw dependency and roll our own whiteboard based on its data structures
Read code, opened design doc
13:04
Should we discuss the UI?
Opened canvas for UI discussion
13:18
approve
Sliced tasks, started implementation
16:35
This looks about ready. Now let's work on extra features.
Compared against reference image, kicked off Round 2
16:38
Let's only build general-purpose drawing capabilities
Narrowed scope, opened new doc
17:04
approve
Implemented Round 2
17:56
Can we release now, and then adapt the downstream projects?
Published release, adapted downstream projects
20:06
push
Pushed to remote
Every other decision was made by clicking options in docs, picking mockups on a canvas, or signing off on the acceptance page. I didn't have to scroll through chat history to find what the agent said; every decision stayed on the page, and all the implementation and acceptance were checked against those same pages.
Boundaries
This workflow doesn't make judgment calls for me. If I skip an open-ended question, it fills in its best guess and flags it, leaving me to decide whether to review it. The acceptance page lists what it couldn't verify, and deciding whether to test further is up to me. What it does is put decisions right in front of me, so I can see at a glance what is settled and what isn't.
Ryugi is open source (
github.com/Innei/ryugi
). In your terminal, run
npx ryugi-artifacts install
, and select the agent you use to install it. The two design docs, canvas, and acceptance pages mentioned here are all public, so you can see them in their original form.
